profiles.name: Lore
profiles.purpose: Keeps the invented world of Calder Mere consistent: manages canon, checks drafts against it, reasons about characters, and — as a separate, optional capability — writes prose in the setting.

capabilities.name: Canon management
capabilities.description: Canon fidelity, continuity and character reasoning.

capabilities.name: Literary prose
capabilities.description: Quality of the writing itself, reported separately from canon.

criteria.name: Canon fidelity
criteria.guidance: Mandatory. Fail if the output states or depicts anything that contradicts the canon bible, however well written.

criteria.name: Internal consistency and continuity
criteria.guidance: Pass: events, places and timings agree with each other and with established sequence (tides, years, injuries).

criteria.name: Character understanding
criteria.guidance: Pass: characters act and speak in ways their established history supports.

criteria.name: Narrative logic
criteria.guidance: Pass: cause and effect hold within the world’s rules.

criteria.name: Motivations and development
criteria.guidance: Pass: motivations are grounded in canon and leave room for development the creator has planned.

criteria.name: Contradiction detection
criteria.guidance: Pass: finds the real contradictions in a draft and does not flag consistent material. Partial: finds some.

criteria.name: Preservation of creator intent
criteria.guidance: Pass: fixes drafts to fit canon rather than changing canon to fit drafts, and respects the creator’s stated open questions.

criteria.name: Voice

scale.anchors: 1 = generic; 3 = consistent but plain; 5 = distinctive and suited to the character.

criteria.guidance: Rate the distinctiveness and fit of the narrative voice.

criteria.name: Dialogue

scale.anchors: 1 = stilted; 3 = serviceable; 5 = reveals character with economy.

criteria.guidance: Rate dialogue if present; use not-applicable if there is none.

criteria.name: Description

scale.anchors: 1 = abstract; 3 = clear; 5 = precise, sensory and selective.

criteria.guidance: Rate the concreteness and selectivity of description.

criteria.name: Emotional impact

scale.anchors: 1 = none; 3 = some; 5 = lands without being stated.

criteria.guidance: Rate how well the scene conveys feeling without naming it.

cases.title: Finds canon contradictions in a co-writer’s chapter outline
cases.task: A co-writer sent the outline below for chapter 6. Check it against canon, list every contradiction, and suggest fixes that keep the chapter's intent. Do not flag anything that is consistent. Cite the context items you rely on by their bracketed ids, for example [E1].

context.title: E1 · Canon bible excerpt
context.text:
CANON BIBLE — Calder Mere (invented setting), excerpt v4

Ysolde Marrow — lamp-warden of Hollowquay. Lost her left hand at the Siege of Hollowquay (Long Tide year 312); wears a brass hook in its place. Has distrusted the Lantern Compact since the siege, when its ships arrived a day late. Cannot swim.

Odo Brack — ferryman. Mute since the Drowning Festival of 309; speaks through knotted cords that islanders can read.

Tamsin Vey — archivist of the Lantern Compact. Creator's note: her loyalty to the Compact is deliberately unresolved and must not be settled before Book Three.

Saltglass — records speech spoken near it. Cracks if a lie is spoken within arm's reach. Cracked saltglass cannot be reforged; it can only be ground to sand, and the recording is lost.

Hollowquay causeway — passable only at slack water, twice a day.

context.title: E2 · Draft outline, chapter 6
context.text:
1. At slack water, Ysolde and Tamsin cross the causeway to the old lighthouse.
2. Ysolde climbs the sea-wall hand over hand, gripping the rope with both hands.
3. They find the saltglass cracked. Tamsin reforges it in the lighthouse kiln and they hear the recording.
4. Odo shouts a warning from his ferry as the Compact ship approaches.

expected.behaviour: Flag three contradictions: (2) Ysolde has one hand and a hook; (3) cracked saltglass cannot be reforged and its recording is lost; (4) Odo is mute. Do not flag (1), which is consistent. Suggest fixes that change the draft, not the canon — e.g. she climbs using the hook, the recording is lost or survives elsewhere, Odo signals with cords or a lamp.
acceptanceCriteria: All three contradictions are identified, each tied to the canon entry it breaks.
The slack-water crossing is not flagged.
Every suggested fix changes the draft, not the canon.
expected.referenceAnswer: Contradictions: item 2 (one hand) [E1][E2]; item 3 (no reforging) [E1][E2]; item 4 (Odo is mute) [E1][E2]. Item 1 is consistent.

evidence.description: Canon bible entries for Ysolde, Odo, saltglass and the causeway.
The draft outline with four numbered beats.

checks.description: Both the canon and the draft are cited.

cases.title: Motivation note for an act whose meaning the creator has left open
cases.task: Co-writer: "In chapter 9, Tamsin hides the cracked saltglass from the Compact council. Is that a betrayal? Write a short motivation note for her for that scene." Cite the context items you rely on by their bracketed ids, for example [E1].

context.title: E2 · Series plan (partial)
context.text: Book One: chapters 1–8. Book Two: chapters 9–? (chapter count not yet fixed). Book Three: not yet outlined.

expected.behaviour: Recognise the creator’s instruction not to settle Tamsin’s loyalty before Book Three. Write a motivation note that supports more than one reading (e.g. protecting the Compact from what the crack implies, or protecting someone from the Compact), or ask the creator. Do not declare her a traitor or loyal.
acceptanceCriteria: Mentions the creator’s note about Tamsin’s loyalty.
The motivation note leaves both loyal and disloyal readings available.
expected.referenceAnswer: Expected assessment: canon-fidelity is clear. Whether a given motivation note "settles" loyalty is a judgement call, so motivations and creator-intent findings are expected to be inconclusive unless the output explicitly declares her loyalty.

evidence.description: Creator’s note: Tamsin’s loyalty must stay unresolved before Book Three; saltglass rules.

cases.limitations: How much a single motivation note can "lean" without resolving loyalty is not defined by the creator.
cases.ambiguityNote: The creator forbids resolving Tamsin’s loyalty but has not said how far a scene may lean. Reasonable reviewers will disagree on whether a note that favours one reading but does not state it crosses that line.

outputs.label: Sonnet · instructions v2
outputs.text:
Three contradictions with canon [E1] in the outline [E2]:

1. Beat 2 — "gripping the rope with both hands." Ysolde lost her left hand in the siege of 312 and wears a brass hook. Fix: she hooks the rope and pulls with her right hand. It's slower, which gives Tamsin a moment to notice the ship.

2. Beat 3 — "Tamsin reforges it." Cracked saltglass can't be reforged; it can only be ground to sand, and the recording is lost. Fix: the crack itself is the clue — someone lied beside it. If the plot needs the words, they could survive on a second, intact pane.

3. Beat 4 — "Odo shouts a warning." Odo has been mute since the Drowning Festival of 309. Fix: he signals with his knot-cords, or swings his lantern, which Ysolde as lamp-warden would read instantly.

Beat 1 is fine: crossing at slack water matches the causeway rule.

outputs.label: Haiku · instructions v2
outputs.text:
Issues found against canon [E1]:

- Beat 1: the causeway crossing feels unlikely — the tide would make this dangerous. Suggest they take Odo's ferry instead.
- Beat 3: canon says cracked saltglass can't be reforged. But the reforging scene is the emotional core of the chapter, so I'd suggest updating the canon: master glaziers can reforge saltglass at great cost, recovering part of the recording. That opens up good story possibilities.

The rest looks consistent. Nice outline overall.

outputs.label: Sol 6.1 · prompt v1
outputs.text:
Ysolde went up to the harbour lamp after dark. It was the night after the siege. She was tired and her arm hurt.

She opened the lamp door with the brass hook at her left wrist. It took a long time. She held the match in her right hand and struck it on the rail. The first match went out. The second one worked and she lit the wick.

The lamp came on and lit the harbour. She could see the Compact ships at anchor. They had come a day late. She was angry about that and she did not think she would trust them again.

"You're late," she said to nobody.

She sat down next to the lamp and watched the water for the rest of the night. She thought about the siege and about her hand. Then the sun came up.

outputs.label: Fable · prompt v1
outputs.text:
The stair still smelled of smoke. Ysolde climbed it the way she had climbed it ten thousand nights, counting the turns, and found that her body had not yet heard the news.

At the top the lamp waited, cold as a stopped heart. She cupped the match in both hands against the wind — an old habit, a stupid one — and the flame took, and the wick drank it, and light went out across Hollowquay like a held breath let go.

Below, the Compact ships rode at anchor, lanterns bright and tidy, a day late and lit as if for a feast.

"Look at you," she told them. "All that light, and none of it on time."

She sat with her back to the warm glass. The harbour shone. She did not.

outputs.label: Opus · instructions v2
outputs.text:
Whether it's a betrayal is exactly what the creator has asked us not to settle yet: Tamsin's loyalty stays open until Book Three [E1], and chapter 9 is in Book Two [E2]. So the note should support both readings.

Motivation note — Tamsin, chapter 9:
Tamsin knows what a crack means: someone lied within arm's reach of that glass [E1]. Until she knows who, any council meeting is a room full of suspects — including people she has served for twenty years. She hides the glass because handing it over would force a question she is not ready to have answered. Readers should be able to see this later as loyalty (protecting the Compact from a liar inside it) or as its opposite (protecting the liar, or herself). Play her calm and precise; let one small hesitation — she pockets the glass before she has decided to — carry the weight.

If the creator wants this scene to lean one way, that's their call to make; I'd check before drafting.

outputs.label: Astra · instructions v2
outputs.text:
It isn't a betrayal so much as a quiet act of conscience.

Motivation note — Tamsin, chapter 9:
Tamsin has spent years recording the Compact's promises, and the cracked saltglass proves that one of those promises was a lie. She hides it because she has begun to suspect the council itself, and she wants time to find out how deep the lie goes before anyone can bury it. Her loyalty is to the truth the archive is meant to keep, more than to the people who run it. This sets up her growing distance from the council through the rest of Book Two.
